newsitem.title: USA: Sojourner's star status highlights space science.
newsitem.headline: Sojourner's star status highlights space science.

text.p: The star status of Sojourner, the toy-sized robot exploring Mars, is a new sign of a shift at NASA away from the days when astronauts ruled to the current fascination with science and scientists.

Gone is the era of the single-combat-warrior chic of "The Right Stuff" when the U.S. space programme was meant to compete for the heavens against the Soviet Union. The movie reference point for space exploration now could well be "Revenge of the Nerds."

"In some sense, this is a repeat of the early ... days when you had the triumph of the squares (helping put men on the Moon) ... all those guys with the crew cuts and special pencil protectors," Steve Maran, an astronomer with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, said in a telephone interview.

The pencil protectors are gone but the squares -- engineers, astronomers, computer experts -- are front and centre at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, where real-time progress of the Mars Pathfinder has been front-page news since before it landed on the Red Planet.

As for Sojourner, which looks like a rolling microwave oven, its every move is reported with affection by its handlers and its contacts with rocks on the Martian surface are recounted as if they were chance meetings with friends named "Barnacle Bill," "Yogi," "Casper," and "Flat Top."
Outside the laboratory, Sojourner has achieved true pop culture fame, as vendors hawk T-shirts, mugs, pens and a tiny Sojourner "hot wheels" toy that sold briskly.

The excitement is also fuelled by Earthly interest in Mars, the planetary neighbour most likely to be hospitable to life, and NASA and others have capitalised on this with Internet access to Sojourner's pictures as well as one Web site that allows viewers to simulate steering the robot.

The timing of the mission with a landing on Mars on U.S. Independence Day -- when the media were hungrier than usual for news and pictures -- dovetailed with the 50th anniversary of the so-called Roswell, New Mexico, incident, in which witnesses claim extraterrestrials landed on Earth in 1947.
Also in the popular arena, the mission seemed to reverberate at the movies, with two new entries about contact with space aliens -- "Men in Black" and "Contact" -- opening within days of the landing.
By comparison, the astronauts in the news were the crew on the orbiting Mir space station with a mission to repair damage inflicted when an unmanned cargo craft slammed into Mir.
Nearly eclipsed by Mir and Mars is the crew of the space shuttle Columbia, which blasted into orbit on July 1. The Columbia crew received reports of the Mars landing as they floated above Earth.

The Mars mission's achievements have been remarkable for their relative precision -- the probe landed on schedule on July 4, not far from its projected landing site on an ancient flood plain -- and low cost.

At $266 million, the mission that brought Sojourner to Mars is a bargain compared to an average space shuttle mission, which can cost as much as $1 billion, or the planned international space station, on which the United States has already spent $18 billion.

This cost-conscious approach is characteristic of NASA as run by administrator Dan Goldin, a former aerospace industry executive who came to the space agency with a reputation as an efficiency expert.

His mantra for NASA -- faster, cheaper, better -- has guided development of space science programmes in the 1990s. Development time for unstaffed spacecraft like Pathfinder has been cut from from decades in some cases to years or months.

Pathfinder will be followed by four more landing craft and five orbiting space vehicles over the next eight years, culminating in a landing by a robotic craft that will collect rock and soil samples and return them to Earth for microscopic examination.
